title: Behaviour of Gases

cards.title: 5.1 Gaseous State and the Classical Gas Laws
body: 5.1 Gaseous State and the Classical Gas Laws

**The Gaseous State** is defined as one of the fundamental states of matter characterized by a lack of definite shape or volume, low density, high compressibility, and the rapid, random, and constant motion of its constituent particles.

Physically, gases behave very differently from solids and liquids due to the vast distances separating their individual molecules. Because intermolecular forces are weak in this state, gases expand spontaneously to completely fill any container in which they are placed. This low particle density means gases are highly compressible; applying an external force easily reduces the space between gas molecules, drastically decreasing the gas's volume. cards.title: Behaviour of Gases
body: **Charles's Law**, formulated by Jacques Charles in 1787, states that at constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature: $$V \\propto T \\implies \\frac{V}{T} = k$$. This relationship is calculated using the formula: $\frac{V_1}{T_1} = \frac{V_2}{T_2}$. Extrapolating a plot of volume versus temperature in Celsius down to zero volume reveals a theoretical lower limit of temperature at $$-273.15^\circ\\text{C}$$, designated as absolute zero ($$0\\text{ K}$$), where all molecular motion ceases. **Avogadro's Law**, formulated by Amedeo Avogadro in 1811, states that at constant temperature and pressure, equal volumes of all gases contain an equal number of moles: $$V \\propto n \\implies \\frac{V}{n} = k$$, or $\frac{V_1}{n_1} = \frac{V_2}{n_2}$. cards.title: Behaviour of Gases
body: > **💡 Did You Know?**: When you inhale, your diaphragm moves down, increasing the volume of your lungs. According to Boyle's Law, this volume increase drops the pressure inside your lungs below atmospheric pressure, forcing air to rush in! Breathing is literally a direct application of Boyle's Law!

> **🧠 Pro-Tip**: To easily remember which variables are held constant in each of the three classical laws, think of: **B**oyle's Law holds **T**emperature constant (**B**oiling water is hot), **C**harles's Law holds **P**ressure constant (**C**harles is under **P**ressure), and **G**ay-Lussac's Law holds **V**olume constant (**G**allon is a unit of **V**olume).

cards.title: 5.2 Ideal Gas Law, Kinetic Molecular Theory, and Real Gas Deviations
body: 5.2 Ideal Gas Law, Kinetic Molecular Theory, and Real Gas Deviations

**The Ideal Gas Law** is defined as a physical law describing the relationship between the four state variables of an ideal gas ($$P$$, $$V$$, $$n$$ and $$T$$) through a single equation of state: $$ PV = nRT $$, where $$R$$ is the universal gas constant.

By combining Boyle's Law ($$V \\propto \\frac{1}{P}$$), Charles's Law ($$V \\propto T$$), and Avogadro's Law ($$V \\propto n$$), we derive the single relationship: $$V \\propto \\frac{nT}{P}$$. Introducing a constant of proportionality yields the Ideal Gas Law: $$PV = nRT$$. The constant $$R$$ is the Universal Gas Constant, and its value depends on the units of pressure and volume. To mathematically describe the physical behavior of a gas, chemists monitor four state variables: pressure ($$P$$), volume ($$V$$), temperature ($$T$$), and amount of substance ($$n$$) measured in moles. Pressure is defined as the force exerted per unit area by gas molecules colliding with the container walls. Volume represents the space occupied by the gas, which is always equal to the volume of the containing vessel. Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the gas particles, and must always be expressed on an absolute scale, namely the Kelvin scale ($$T(\\text{K}) = T(^\circ\\text{C}) + 273.15$$), to ensure gas law calculations are physically valid.

cards.title: Behaviour of Gases
body: When a fixed mass of gas undergoes simultaneous changes in pressure, volume, and temperature, Boyle's and Charles's laws are combined to form the **Combined Gas Law**: $$\frac{PV}{T} = k$$. For transitions between two physical states, the law is written as: $$\frac{P_1V_1}{T_1} = \frac{P_2V_2}{T_2}$$. This relationship is incredibly useful for weather balloons, scuba diving tanks, and high-altitude flight engineering, where temperature, volume, and pressure fluctuate simultaneously.

cards.problem: Under which of the following physical conditions does a real gas behave most like a theoretically perfect ideal gas?

steps.text: Ideal behavior assumes negligible molecular volume and zero intermolecular attractive forces.
**Step 2: Identify conditions that minimize these factors**
Low pressure keeps molecules far apart (making molecular volume negligible). High temperature keeps molecules moving rapidly (overcoming weak attractive forces).

cards.title: Study Notes worked
cards.problem: Which of the following gases is expected to behave most ideally under standard conditions due to having the weakest intermolecular attractive forces?

steps.text: $$H_2O$$ and $$NH_3$$ have strong hydrogen bonding. $$CO_2$$ is nonpolar but relatively large, with moderate London dispersion forces. Helium ($$He$$) is a tiny, nonpolar single atom.
The weaker the intermolecular forces, the more ideally a gas behaves. Helium has the weakest attractive forces.

cards.title: Behaviour of Gases
body: The relationship between these variables was established through empirical laws. **Boyle's Law**, formulated by Robert Boyle in 1662, states that at a constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure: $$V \\propto \\frac{1}{P} \\implies PV = k$$. For a system undergoing a change in pressure or volume at constant temperature, we apply the formula: $$P_1V_1 = P_2V_2$$. Graphically, plotting $$P$$ against $$V$$ yields a hyperbola known as an isotherm. At the molecular level, decreasing the container's volume crowds the gas molecules closer together, increasing the frequency of their collisions with the container walls, which macosopically increases the measured pressure.

| Gas Law | Constant Variables | Mathematical Relation | Practical Formula |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Boyle's Law** | Temperature ($$T$$), moles ($$n$$) | Inverse: $$V \\propto \\frac{1}{P}$$ | $$P_1V_1 = P_2V_2$$ |
| **Charles's Law** | Pressure ($$P$$), moles ($$n$$) | Direct: $$V \\propto T$$ | $$\frac{V_1}{T_1} = \frac{V_2}{T_2}$$ |
| **Avogadro's Law** | Temperature ($$T$$), Pressure ($$P$$) | Direct: $$V \\propto n$$ | $$\frac{V_1}{n_1} = \frac{V_2}{n_2}$$ |
| **Combined Gas Law** | Moles of gas ($$n$$) | Combined: $$V \\propto \\frac{T}{P}$$ | $$\frac{P_1V_1}{T_1} = \frac{P_2V_2}{T_2}$$ |

cards.title: Behaviour of Gases
body: To explain these macroscopic gas properties at a microscopic, molecular level, chemists developed the Kinetic Molecular Theory of Gases (KMT). This theory is built on five core postulates: 1) Gases consist of extremely tiny particles (atoms or molecules) separated by vast empty spaces, meaning the actual volume of the gas particles is completely negligible compared to the total volume of the container; 2) Gas particles are in constant, rapid, random straight-line motion, colliding with each other and the container walls; 3) The collisions between gas particles and with the container walls are perfectly elastic, meaning there is no net loss of kinetic energy during collisions; 4) There are no attractive or repulsive intermolecular forces between gas particles; 5) The average kinetic energy of gas particles is directly proportional to the absolute temperature ($$K.E. \\propto T$$).
